nameStory: The 'grass pea' name comes from this plant's slender, grass-like appearance when not in bloom, with its narrow stems and small leaves that can blend right into grassy areas. The 'round-seeded vetchling' name refers to its spherical seeds (sphaericus means 'sphere-shaped' in Latin) and its membership in the vetchling group - climbing or sprawling pea relatives.
description: Grass pea is a small annual flowering plant that grows just 6 to 12 inches tall, making it easy to overlook among other vegetation. This Mediterranean native belongs to the legume family, the same group that includes beans, peas, and clovers. Its most striking feature is its distinctive brick-red flowers that stand out beautifully against its delicate, almost grass-like foliage. With only one confirmed sighting in New England, this is truly a rare find for local plant enthusiasts.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Distinctive brick-red flowers shaped like tiny sweet pea blossoms, with the characteristic pea-family structure of a banner petal, two wing petals, and a keel

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Low-growing annual that reaches only 6-12 inches tall, with a delicate, almost wispy appearance that can easily blend into surrounding grasses

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Small, narrow leaflets arranged in pairs along slender stems, giving the plant its grass-like appearance when flowers aren't visible

idTips.label: Seeds
idTips.description: Round, sphere-shaped seeds develop in small pods typical of the pea family - you can feel their roundness by gently rolling them between your fingers

habitat: Look for grass pea in disturbed, sunny locations with dry, nutrient-rich soils such as roadsides, field edges, or areas with recent soil disturbance. It prefers open habitats where it won't be shaded out by taller plants. Given its Mediterranean origins and extreme rarity in New England, any sighting would likely be in warmer, protected microclimates in southern New England.

seasonality.spring: Seeds germinate and young plants begin growing as an annual, developing their characteristic grass-like foliage first.
seasonality.summer: The distinctive brick-red flowers bloom during the warm months, making this the best time for positive identification of this rare species.
seasonality.fall: Plants complete their lifecycle by producing the round seeds that give this species its scientific name, then die back as winter approaches.
seasonality.winter: No above-ground parts persist - seeds overwinter in the soil and may germinate the following spring if conditions are right.

funFact: This tiny plant is so rare in New England that it has been spotted only once in the entire region - making any encounter with grass pea like finding a botanical unicorn in your own backyard!
confusionNotes: The grass-like foliage could be mistaken for actual grasses or sedges when not in bloom, but the distinctive brick-red pea flowers immediately set it apart. Other Lathyrus species in New England have different colored flowers - purple, pink, yellow, or white - making the brick-red blooms a dead giveaway.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'grass pea,' this plant is actually a legume (bean family member) and not related to true grasses at all. The name simply refers to its grass-like appearance when the distinctive flowers aren't visible.
compareHints: Grass pea stands out from its New England Lathyrus cousins primarily by its unique brick-red flowers - no other sweet pea or vetchling in our region shares this color. It's also much smaller than most relatives like broad-leaved sweet pea or seaside pea. The combination of tiny stature, grass-like leaves, and those unmistakable rusty-red blooms makes this species unmistakable once you know what to look for.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's Lathyrus species, seaside pea is the only one with those distinctive thick, waxy blue-green leaves and strict beach habitat.
Among New England's sweet peas, broad-leaved sweet pea stands out with its distinctly wide leaflets - most others like meadow pea have narrow, grass-like leaflets.
Among New England's wild peas, narrow-leaved everlasting-pea stands out with its bold pink flowers and strongly winged stems.
Among New England's wild peas, meadow pea stands out with its bright yellow flowers - most of its relatives like seaside pea and marsh pea have purple or pink blooms.
Among its Lathyrus relatives, marsh pea is distinguished by its wetland habitat and pinkish-purple flowers.

Unlike the broad-leaved sweet pea which has wider leaflets and no tubers, or the seaside pea which has 6-12 leaflets, tuberous pea is distinguished by its simple two-leaflet arrangement and underground tuber system.
Unlike its Lathyrus relatives in New England, spring vetch lacks the climbing tendrils found on species like broad-leaved sweet pea and narrow-leaved everlasting-pea.
Among its Lathyrus relatives in New England, sweet pea stands out for its incredible fragrance and annual growth habit.

Among its Lathyrus relatives in New England, pale vetchling stands out for its uniquely subdued flower color – while seaside pea has purple flowers, meadow pea is bright yellow, and broad-leaved sweet pea shows off in magenta.
